A checklist for testing. A defined method for managing risks. A review before approval. A record for changes. A dashboard for metrics. A meeting to discuss the metrics. And sometimes, another meeting to discuss why the first meeting didn't solve the metric. If you've worked in a large software, engineering, consulting, product, or service organization, you may recognize the feeling. At first, a process-driven workplace can feel frustrating. You may wonder: “ Why can't we just do the work? ” But there is another way to look at it. Imagine an organization where one brilliant employee can solve almost any problem. Now imagine that employee leaves. What happens? If the organization's success leaves with the employee, the organization doesn't really own the capability. It borrowed it. That is one of the fundamental problems process maturity tries to solve. A mature organization attempts to turn individual knowledge into organizational capability. It tries to transform: “John knows how to do this.” into: “Our organization knows how to do this.” And that difference becomes enormous as an organization grows. This is where concepts such as CMMI, process maturity, quality management, organizational processes, metrics, governance, risk management, and continuous improvement become important. CMMI's current framework describes maturity as a staged path for organizational performance and process improvement, progressing from Initial through Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, and Optimizing. But there is a deeper question. Why do human beings sometimes resist processes that are designed to help them? The answer has as much to do with psychology as it does with management. --- The Real Meaning of a Process-Driven Environment A process-driven organization is not simply an organization with lots of documents. It is an organization where important work is guided by defined, repeatable, measurable, and improvable ways of working. Consider two software teams. Team A A customer reports a critical production problem. One engineer investigates it. Another engineer starts making changes. A manager calls someone. Someone creates an email thread. Nobody is quite sure who owns the incident. Eventually, the issue is fixed. Everyone celebrates. Three months later, almost exactly the same problem happens again. The team asks: “Who knows how we solved this last time?” Silence. --- Team B The same incident occurs. The workflow is already known: Incident reported ↓ Incident logged ↓ Severity assigned ↓ Owner identified ↓ Impact assessed ↓ Root cause investigated ↓ Corrective action ↓ Testing ↓ Approval ↓ Deployment ↓ Closure ↓ Lessons learned ↓ Process improvement The second team isn't necessarily smarter. It simply has a system that helps convert experience into organizational memory. That is the power of process. A process-driven organization tries to make successful outcomes repeatable rather than dependent on individual heroics. --- CMMI and Process-Driven Environment Are Not the Same Thing This distinction is important. CMMI is a model/framework for improving organizational capability and performance. A process-driven environment is a way of operating. An organization can be process-driven without having a formal CMMI appraisal. And having CMMI-related documentation doesn't automatically mean an organization has a mature process culture. CMMI appraisals are intended to examine strengths and weaknesses in an organization's processes and how closely those processes relate to CMMI best practices. Current CMMI material also emphasizes performance improvement rather than merely checking whether documents exist. This leads to one of the most important ideas in process management: Documentation is evidence of a process. It is not the purpose of the process. --- Why Organizations Become Process-Driven Think about a five-person company. Everyone knows everyone. If the customer has a problem, the customer calls the founder. If a developer needs approval, they ask the team lead. If someone needs historical information, they ask the person who remembers it. It works. Until the company becomes 500 people. Then 5,000. Then 50,000. Suddenly: Informal knowledge doesn't scale. The organization needs a shared operating system. That operating system may include: - Standard processes - Defined responsibilities - Policies - Procedures - Templates - Governance - Metrics - Quality controls - Risk management - Change management - Reviews - Organizational knowledge - Continuous improvement The larger the organization becomes, the more expensive inconsistency can become.
